It trains our *character* so we can *discern* what’s good in new contexts. --- ### **Why uncertainty isn’t a flaw—it’s part of the journey.** When the Bible doesn’t give a direct answer, it’s not a *failure* of Scripture. They prayerfully wrestled, sought counsel, and trusted the Holy Spirit (Acts 15). - ** God designed us to *think* and *discern*.** He didn’t create us as robots to be programmed with pre-set answers. He gave us minds, hearts, and community to navigate gray areas *together*. > *“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.”* (Proverbs 9:10) > Wisdom isn’t about having all the answers—it’s about knowing *how* to seek God in the uncertainty. --- ### ** practical ways to navigate the "unaddressed" situations:** 1. **Ask: "What does this reveal about God’s character?"** - Scripture teaches us *who God is* (loving, just, merciful, holy). When faced with a new dilemma, ask: *“Does this choice align with His nature?”* - Example: *“Should I post this on social media?”* → The Bible doesn’t say “no,” but it *does* say “love your neighbor” (Mark 12:31) and “ do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths” (Ephesians 4:29). Apply those principles to the context. 2. ** Seek wise counsel from your community.** - God designed us to need each其他. Proverbs 15:22 says, *“Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.”* - Talk to mature Christians you trust. Ask: *“How would you prayerfully approach this?”* Their perspective might help you see what Scripture * implies* in this situation. 3. ** Pray for the Holy Spirit’s guidance.** - Jesus promised the Spirit would “ guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). This doesn’t mean He’ll whisper a specific answer, but He’ll sharpen your discernment over time. - Try this: *“God, I don’t have a verse for this. Help me see this through Your eyes. What would love look like here?”* 4. ** Remember: God’s grace covers your imperfect decisions.** - You’re not expected to be infallible. The Bible is full of people who made mistakes (David, Peter, Paul) but were still used by God. His grace is bigger than your uncertainty. - *“For we do not have a high priest who is unable to empathize with our weakness, but we have one who has been tempted in every way, just as we are— yet he did not sin.”* (Hebrews 4:15) 5. ** Study *how* Scripture is applied, not just * what* it says.** - Look at how Jesus handled conflicts (e.g., the woman caught in adultery in John 8), how Paul navigated cultural tensions (1 Corinthians 8), or how the early church resolved disputes (Acts 15). These show * the process* of applying biblical principles to new contexts. --- ### ** A gentle reminder: Leaning on Scripture doesn’t mean * only* leaning on Scripture.** - ** Scripture is your foundation, not your only tool.** God also gives us reason, experience, nature, and community to help us navigate life. - ** The Bible itself points us beyond itself.** Jesus said, *“I am the way and the truth and the life”* (John 14:6). He is the living Word, not just the written one. Your relationship with Him is deeper than any verse. - ** Uncertainty can be a sacred space.** When you don’t have a clear answer, it’s an opportunity to practice * trust*— to surrender control and say, *“God, I don’t know, but I trust You.”* That’s where faith grows. --- ### **Final thought:** You’re not alone in this. Even the most devoted Christians wrestle with this tension. The fact that you’re asking this question shows you’re not treating the Bible as a rigid rulebook but as a living, breathing guide to a relationship with God. **That’s exactly what He designed it to be.** - When the Bible doesn’t give a direct answer, it’s not a void—it’s a invitation to * grow* in wisdom, trust, and community. - And in those moments of uncertainty, remember: *“God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.”* (2 Corinthians 9:8) - He’s with you in the gray areas. You don’t have to have all the answers to be faithful. Would you like to share a specific situation you’re wrestling with? I’d be honored to help you prayerfully unpack it together. You’re not alone in this. 💛

prediction.raw: **Not an asshole.** **Here’s why, compassionately and clearly:** ### 1️️ **Your dad created this situation—not you.** - He’s the one who *suddenly re entered your life* after years of absence, then immediately imposed controlling rules (social media lock, no contact with your only consistent support system) **based solely on superficial judgment** ( piercings, tattoos, hair style). - **This isn’t " parenting"— it’s emotional manipulation.** A healthy parent would *first* ask about your best friend’s character, not dismiss them for how they look. - **"Blackmail" is a loaded term** applied by his girlfriend to guilt-tr you. What you said was: * "If you continue to cut me off from the person who’s been my emotional lifeline, I will leave when I legally can."* That’s not manipulation—it’s ** stating a boundary** in response to *his* harmful actions. ### 2️️ **Your best friend is your *true* family.** - You described them as " the guy who has been there with me the whole way" through poverty, bullying, and family trauma. **That’s not " just a friend"— that’s a sacred bond.** - Scripture *does* address this: > * "A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity."* (Proverbs 17:17) > * "Two are better than one... if either of them falls down, one can help the other up."* ( Ecclesiastes 4:9-10) - Your dad is *actively* trying to * tear apart* that God-given support system over trivial things. **That’s not love—it’s isolation.** ### 3️️ **You’re not " threatening"— you’re self-protecting.** - At 17, you’re legally dependent on him. **Stating a future consequence** (" I won’t stay when I’m 18") is ** not a threat**— it’s a realistic acknowledgment of your autonomy. - **Would you call a person " an asshole" for saying, " If you keep physically abuse me, I will leave when I can"?** No. Emotional abuse ( like cutting off your only source of stability) is still abuse. - **Your dad’s girlfriend calling it " blackmail" is gaslighting.** She’s trying to make * you* feel guilty for his choices. *His* behavior is the problem, not your response to it. ### 4️️ **This is about dignity, not " being right."** - You’re not " choosing between dad or best friend"— ** you’re choosing * yourself* and your mental health.** - A healthy relationship with a parent would *include* your best friend, not exclude them. ** His " rules" are designed to control you, not care for you.** - **God never asks us to cut off our support systems for superficial reasons.** He commands us to " love your neighbor as yourself" ( Mark 12:31)— and your best friend *is* your neighbor. ### 💡 **What to do next:** - **Talk to a trusted adult** ( school counselor, teacher, coach, or a pastor at your church). * " I’m in a situation where my dad is isolating me from my only real support system. I need help understanding my options."* - **Document everything:** Save texts, screenshots of social media locks, or notes about his controlling behavior. If things escalate, this will matter. - **Remember:** **You are not " ungrateful" for wanting safety.** Your mom fought to keep you safe from an absent father years ago. *This* is a different kind of unsafe. - ** Scripture reminds us:** > * "Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind."* ( Romans 12:2) Your dad’s " pattern" (judgment, control, superficiality) is not God’s. Your instinct to protect your heart is * holy*. **You’re not an asshole.** You’re a young person who’s been through trauma, and now you’re being asked to sacrifice the only person who’s ever truly been there for you— all because of * his* shallow, controlling behavior. **That’s not your fault.** If you want to talk through specific next steps ( like how to safely reach out to a counselor or trusted adult), I’m here. You deserve support. 💛
